lesson.title: Votes for Favors: How Political Machines Ran the Gilded Age City
lesson.summary: In the chaotic, rapidly growing cities of the late nineteenth century, informal political organizations called machines filled the gap left by weak city governments, trading jobs, favors, and services for votes, and often turning public office into private profit.
lesson.body:
The explosive growth described in the story of Urbanization left city governments badly overmatched. Formal government struggled to keep pace with the flood of new residents, many of them immigrants who spoke little English, had no money to fall back on, and had no experience navigating American law, courts, or bureaucracy. Political machines stepped into that gap, offering informal help that official government did not.

A typical machine was organized like a pyramid, running from precinct captains and ward bosses at the neighborhood level up to a single citywide boss at the top. Precinct captains often knew every family on their block personally: they helped find jobs, delivered coal in the winter, helped with legal trouble, and even paid for funerals, and in return expected the loyalty of those families' votes on election day.

Machines built directly on the logic of the spoils system, the practice of rewarding political loyalty with government jobs rather than merit, and took it to an extreme at the city level. Machine loyalists filled police forces, sanitation departments, and other city offices, while city contracts for construction and supplies routinely went to businesses willing to kick back money or political support to the machine in charge.

Machines had a genuinely double character. For many immigrant families, a machine's ward boss provided real, tangible help that no other institution offered in an era with almost no public welfare system. At the same time, machines siphoned enormous sums of public money through bribery, graft, and rigged elections, a trade off that made them simultaneously beloved in immigrant neighborhoods and despised by reformers and much of the middle class. No machine would come to embody both sides of that trade off more clearly than New York's Tammany Hall.
